newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal welcomes private operators to railways.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal welcomes private operators to railways.

text.p: Portugal is overhauling its creaking state-owned railway system and inviting private contractors to operate some lines in a crusade to boost efficiency and slash losses.

Under a restructuring plan ending in 2000, the Socialist government will this month split Caminhos de Ferro Portugueses (CP) into two new companies -- one to transport passengers and freight, and another to look after infrastructure.
Comboios de Portugal S.A. will operate rolling stock and Rede Ferroviaria Nacional SA - REFER, E.P. will maintain tracks and stations and control traffic.
The government will also create an independent watchdog to monitor the two concerns, Under-Secretary for Transport Antonio Guilhermino Rodrigues said in a recent interview.
The state will absorb 300 billion escudos ($1.78 billion) of CP's debts, which will not be passed on to the new companies.
MAJOR INVESTMENT PROGRAMME

Portugal will invest 574 billion escudos ($3.4 billion), with the help of European Union funds, to upgrade infrastructure and some 100 billion escudos ($590 million) in new trains by 2000, Guilhermino Rodrigues said. He declined to estimate the total cost of the railways' reorganisation.

In May, the government will launch a public competition for a private contractor to operate a line crossing Lisbon from the southern suburb of Fogueteiro, across the River Tagus, to the northern suburb of Chelas.

"This will be a first experience in terms of opening a concession to private operators. We then plan to offer other lines," Guilhermino Rodrigues told Reuters. "We want as many lines as possible to be financially self-sufficient," he added.

"We are not planning to privatise railway lines. We will offer concessions to private contractors to operate some lines," he said. "The state is committed to providing an efficient public transportation system."
The winning bidder for the north-south Lisbon line was likely to be chosen in the summer of 1998 and to begin operations in the first quarter of 1999.
Private operators will pay REFER, a public company, a fee for maintaining the infrastructure of their concession.

Potential private contractors included consortia involving Portuguese and European concerns, Guilhermino Rodrigues said. Freight services were attracting most interest from possible bidders, he added.
UNIONS OPPOSE RESTRUCTURING
Unions representing Portugal's 15,000 railway workers held a series of strikes in recent months to protest against the restructuring, but caused little disruption to services.

"We are protesting against the restructuring plan and excessive working hours, and demanding improved career structures," Jose Manuel Oliveira of the Federation of Portuguese Railway Workers' Unions told Reuters recently.
Guilhermino Rodrigues said the unions had nothing to fear from the reorganisation as the government had promised to respect workers' rights.
"There won't be any dismissals," he said.
"Whenever you have a reorganisation like this, there are always protests against change. There are always groups who try to create obstacles," he added.
If the railways boosted their efficiency and wooed customers aggressively from other means of transport, new jobs could be created, he said.
"The railways lost their share of the transport market in recent years. They need to respond better to the needs of the customer," Guilhermino Rodrigues said.
Improved efficiency would eventually cut costs, he said.

He forecast that CP would post a loss of some 80 billion escudos ($475 million) this year, compared with a 70 billion escudo ($415 million) loss in 1996, as the reorganisation raised costs in the short term.
The restructuring would cut the railways' losses by half over the next five years, he said. ($1=168.394)
